## Simple explanation

Image segmentation divides an image into meaningful regions. Instead of
assigning one label to the whole image, a segmentation model marks which
pixels belong to each class or object.

## Technical explanation

A segmentation model predicts a label or object identifier for each pixel.
Semantic segmentation labels pixels by class, so separate objects of the
same class share a label. Instance segmentation also distinguishes individual
objects, while panoptic segmentation combines semantic and instance-level
outputs.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Pixel-level outputs are useful when the shape and location of an object
matter, including medical image analysis, robotics, satellite imagery, and
scene understanding. Segmentation systems need suitable masks for training
and evaluation, and can be costly to annotate and compute.

## How it works

An image is processed by a model that produces a score for each class at
each pixel. A decision rule turns those scores into a mask. Some systems
predict one mask per object instead. Evaluation compares predicted masks
with reference annotations, often using measures such as
[Intersection over Union](intersection-over-union-iou.qmd).

## Practical example

A road-scene model could label every pixel as road, vehicle, pedestrian, or
background. A robot could then use those regions to estimate where it can
move and which areas require caution.

## Common misconceptions

- Segmentation is not the same as image classification: it predicts spatial
  regions, not just a whole-image label.
- Semantic segmentation does not necessarily separate two adjacent objects
  of the same class.
- A visually plausible mask is not necessarily accurate; evaluation should
  use appropriate pixel- or region-level metrics.
